old: This is intramolecular chain transfer ("backbiting"). The 1° chain-end radical reaches back through a six-membered cyclic transition state and abstracts an H from the CH2 five carbons away (a 1,5-H shift), giving a more stable 2° radical within the chain. Ethylene then adds at that site, so the four carbons past it become a butyl branch. Intermolecular H transfer between chains gives the long branches.
new: This is intramolecular chain transfer ("backbiting"). The 1° chain-end radical reaches back through a six-membered cyclic transition state and abstracts an H from C5 (counting the radical carbon as C1; a 1,5-H shift), giving a more stable 2° radical within the chain. Ethylene then adds at that site, so the four carbons past it (C1–C4) become a butyl branch. Intermolecular H transfer between chains gives the long branches.
why: 'five carbons away' is four bonds/carbons from the radical; state the C1/C5 numbering explicitly so the butyl count is clear
